title: BEFORE JAMES SAYS “RESIST THE DEVIL,” HE SAYS SOMETHING MANY CHRISTIANS DON’T WANT TO HEAR
paragraphs: BEFORE JAMES SAYS “RESIST THE DEVIL,” HE SAYS SOMETHING MANY CHRISTIANS DON’T WANT TO HEAR

The enemy you keep rebuking may not be the first thing God is asking you to confront. And the verse many believers quote for spiritual warfare contains a command that could change everything about the way you fight.
There is something deeply unsettling about a Christian who knows how to rebuke the devil but has never learned how to surrender to God.
They know what to say when darkness comes.
They know how to declare victory, quote Scripture, pray against attacks, and command the enemy to flee.

They can recognize temptation in other people. They can identify spiritual compromise in the world. They can talk passionately about demons, strongholds, and the authority believers have in Jesus Christ.
But sometimes, when God begins dealing with their own pride, unforgiveness, secret sin, jealousy, bitterness, or unwillingness to obey Him…
Everything suddenly becomes quiet.
Because fighting the devil can feel heroic.
Submitting to God requires humility.
And humility is where the battle becomes painfully personal.
What if the spiritual breakthrough you have been praying for is not waiting on a louder rebuke?
What if God has already shown you something you need to surrender, but you have been too busy fighting what is outside you to confront what is happening inside you?
Stay with me, because the order of one Bible verse exposes something many of us have spent years avoiding.
James 4:7 says:
“Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” — James 4:7, KJV
Read that again.
Slowly.
Notice what James did not say.
He did not begin with, “Resist the devil.”
He began with, “Submit yourselves therefore to God.”
Before resistance comes submission.
Before confronting the enemy, James calls believers to surrender themselves to the Lord.
And those words are not arranged that way by accident.
The New Testament was written in Koine Greek, and the original wording of James 4:7 begins:
Ὑποτάγητε οὖν τῷ θεῷ, ἀντίστητε δὲ τῷ διαβόλῳ, καὶ φεύξεται ἀφ’ ὑμῶν.
Transliterated:
Hypotagēte oun tō theō, antistēte de tō diabolō, kai pheuxetai aph’ hymōn.
A faithful translation is:
“Therefore, submit yourselves to God. But resist the devil, and he will flee from you.”
The word ὑποτάγητε (hypotagēte) comes from hypotassō, meaning to subject oneself or submit to authority.
Here, it is a command.
Not a suggestion for Christians who happen to feel spiritually mature.
Not an optional discipline reserved for pastors, missionaries, or people who have already overcome their struggles.
A command addressed to people who belong to God.
And the word ἀντίστητε (antistēte) comes from anthistēmi, meaning to resist, oppose, or stand against.
James gives both commands.
Submit to God.
Resist the devil.
The order matters because James is not describing two disconnected spiritual activities. He is calling believers to take their proper position before God while standing against the enemy.
But there is something even more confronting here.
James did not write this verse in isolation.
He was not delivering a motivational slogan about defeating Satan.
He was confronting the spiritual condition of people whose desires were producing conflict, envy, pride, and compromise.
Just a few verses earlier, James asks:
“From whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members?” — James 4:1, KJV
He is talking about desires battling within people.
He is confronting quarrels, selfish ambition, and prayers corrupted by wrong motives.
Then James 4:4 warns about friendship with the world becoming hostility toward God.
This is not a call to hate people who do not believe in Jesus. James is exposing allegiance to a value system that competes with devotion to God.
And then comes James 4:6:
“God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.”
Now the command makes sense.
“Submit yourselves therefore to God.”
That word therefore connects submission to everything James has just said.
God gives grace to the humble.
Therefore, humble yourselves under His authority.
And resist the devil.
Do you see it?
James is not merely teaching believers how to confront evil.
He is showing them how to stop cooperating with the very attitudes that make their lives spiritually divided.
And this is where the passage begins to hurt.
Because it is possible to pray against deception while refusing to be honest.
It is possible to rebuke bitterness while secretly feeding resentment.
It is possible to ask God to remove temptation while deliberately keeping the door open to it.
It is possible to sing about surrender on Sunday while negotiating with disobedience on Monday.
And I wonder how many of us have done exactly that.
Maybe you have been asking God to restore peace in your home, but you refuse to apologize because you believe you were hurt first.
Maybe you have been praying for freedom from lust, but you continue returning to the very content that feeds it.
Maybe you have been asking God to heal your heart, but you have made your pain into an excuse to punish everyone who gets close to you.
Maybe you keep saying, “The devil is attacking my relationships,” when part of the problem is that you will not listen, forgive, speak truthfully, or admit when you are wrong.
Not every hardship is caused by personal sin.
Not every illness, loss, intrusive thought, or season of suffering is evidence that someone has failed to submit to God.
Scripture itself shows righteous people suffering terribly.
Job suffered without the accusations of his friends being true. Paul endured affliction while faithfully serving Christ. Jesus, who was perfectly obedient, suffered more deeply than any of us.
But James will not allow us to blame the devil for everything while refusing to examine our own hearts.
Sometimes the issue is not that you need to shout louder at darkness.
Sometimes you need to tell God the truth.
“Lord, I am angry.”
“Lord, I have become proud.”
“Lord, I keep returning to something You have called me to leave.”
“Lord, I want Your blessings, but I have been resisting Your correction.”
“Lord, I know what Your Word says. I just do not want to obey it.”
That kind of honesty can feel terrifying.
Because we spend so much of our lives trying to appear stronger than we are.
We learn to hide our wounds behind smiles.
We learn to say “God is good” while quietly wondering whether He still wants anything to do with us.
We learn to post Bible verses while wrestling with habits nobody knows about.
We become skilled at appearing spiritually alive while parts of our hearts remain stubbornly closed.
But listen carefully.
God does not call you into the light because He enjoys exposing your shame.
He calls you into the light because darkness is a terrible place to remain.
And the God who commands repentance is also the God who offers mercy.
There is a reason James does not stop at verse 7.
James 4:8 says:
“Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you.”
Then he calls sinners to cleanse their hands and the double-minded to purify their hearts.
James 4:9 speaks of mourning over sin, and verse 10 says:
“Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up.”
This is the movement of the passage.
Not from weakness to self-made spiritual greatness.
But from pride to humility.
From divided loyalty to wholehearted repentance.
From resisting God's correction to receiving His grace.
And from there, standing against the devil.
The call to mourn in this passage is not a command to live in permanent despair. It is a call to take sin seriously rather than treating rebellion as something harmless.
Because genuine repentance is not simply feeling terrible about yourself.
It is turning toward God.
The Greek New Testament often uses the word μετάνοια (metanoia) for repentance, a change of mind or understanding that involves a transformed direction of life.
Repentance is not earning forgiveness through enough tears.
It is no longer defending what God calls sin.
It is bringing your life honestly before the One who has the authority to forgive and transform you.
And that brings us to Jesus.
Because if this article ended with “submit harder, resist harder, and fix yourself,” it would miss the very Gospel that makes real transformation possible.
You cannot save yourself through flawless obedience.
You cannot cleanse your conscience by performing enough religious activities.
You cannot undo your past through determination alone.
You need a Savior.
And Jesus Christ is not merely an example of surrender.
He is the sinless Son of God who obeyed the Father perfectly and gave Himself for sinners.
Think about the wilderness.
Matthew 4 tells us that Jesus was tempted by the devil.
After fasting forty days and forty nights, He was hungry.
The tempter approached Him at a moment of genuine physical weakness.
And what did Jesus do?
He answered temptation with the truth of Scripture.
He refused to use His identity for selfish display.
He refused to worship anyone but God.
He would not abandon His Father's will for the kingdoms of this world.
Matthew 4:10 records Jesus saying:
“Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.”
Then Matthew 4:11 tells us the devil left Him.
Jesus did not defeat temptation by bargaining with it.
He remained faithful to His Father.
And later, in Gethsemane, the depth of His obedience becomes almost unbearable to contemplate.
Facing the suffering ahead, Jesus prayed:
“Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” — Luke 22:42, KJV
Consider those words.
The sinless Savior submitted to the Father's will even as the cross approached.
And on that cross, Jesus bore the judgment our sins deserve.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again.
The resurrection declares that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
This is why Christian surrender is not a desperate attempt to convince God to love us.
It is our response to the Savior who loved us and gave Himself for us.
We do not submit to God to purchase His grace. We submit because His grace has called us out of rebellion and into new life.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes it clear that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works.
And Ephesians 2:10 makes it equally clear that those saved by grace are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace does not make obedience unnecessary.
Grace makes a new life possible.
And perhaps that is what you needed to hear today.
Because somewhere along the way, you began to believe that submitting to God meant losing everything.
Your freedom.
Your identity.
Your future.
Your happiness.
Your control.
And perhaps you have been holding on so tightly to your own plans because you are afraid that if you finally surrender, God will take away the only things that make life bearable.
But what if some of the things you are desperately protecting are the very things keeping you spiritually exhausted?
What if the bitterness you call protection is slowly poisoning your peace?
What if the secret habit you call comfort is deepening your captivity?
What if the pride you call strength is preventing you from receiving correction that could save your relationships?
What if the image you work so hard to maintain is keeping you from experiencing the freedom of being known honestly before God?
Submission to God is not the destruction of your humanity.
It is the rightful surrender of your life to the One who created you, knows you, and redeemed you at the cost of His Son's blood.
And that surrender is not always dramatic.
Sometimes it looks like closing the screen.
Sometimes it looks like deleting a conversation you know is leading you toward sin.
Sometimes it looks like returning what you took.
Sometimes it looks like telling your spouse the truth.
Sometimes it looks like asking forgiveness without adding a speech about why you were justified.
Sometimes it looks like finally seeking help for a struggle you have hidden for years.
Sometimes it looks like refusing to retaliate.
Sometimes it looks like praying through tears when you have no beautiful words left.
And sometimes it looks like whispering:
“Jesus, I cannot keep living like this. I need You.”
That prayer may never impress a crowd.
But it is not insignificant before God.
Psalm 51:17 says:
“A broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.”
David wrote that psalm in the context of grievous sin.
He had no righteous image left to defend before the God who knew everything.
And still, he cried for mercy.
That is the astonishing thing about grace.
God does not require you to pretend your scandal never happened.
He calls you to stop hiding, repent, and come to Him for cleansing.
Think about Peter.
The man who promised loyalty denied Jesus three times.
Imagine the sound of the rooster.
Imagine the terrible recognition that followed.
Imagine knowing that the One you loved had heard your denial.
Luke 22:61–62 describes Peter remembering Jesus' words and going out to weep bitterly.
There are tears that come from embarrassment.
And there are tears that come when the truth about yourself finally breaks through every excuse.
Peter knew what he had done.
But his failure was not the end of his story.
After the resurrection, in John 21, Jesus met Peter again.
The risen Lord questioned Peter about his love and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
Jesus did not pretend the denial was insignificant.
He restored Peter and called him forward.
That is not permission to sin casually.
That is the wonder of undeserved mercy.
The man who denied Jesus was not beyond the reach of Jesus.
And if you are reading this with the weight of a failure you have carried for years, hear what the Gospel actually says.
Your sin is serious.
Your excuses cannot save you.
But your failure does not place you beyond the power of Christ to forgive and restore.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not because confession magically erases consequences.
Not because repentance means every damaged relationship will immediately return to normal.
And not because the past suddenly stops hurting.
But because forgiveness rests on the faithfulness of God and the saving work of Jesus Christ.
Some consequences may remain.
Trust may need to be rebuilt.
Wounds may require time, accountability, and wise support.
Yet the mercy of Christ is real.
And His transforming work is not limited to people with spotless histories.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
Not because Jesus calls evil good.
Not because He hides the truth.
But because He can redeem sinners, restore the repentant, and create a future that is no longer ruled by the guilt of yesterday.
And now we need to return to something James said.
“Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.”
This is a genuine biblical promise.
But it is not a guarantee that believers will never face temptation again, never experience spiritual conflict, or never suffer.
Even after Jesus resisted the devil in the wilderness, Luke 4:13 says the devil departed from Him “for a season.”
The Christian life requires ongoing watchfulness.
First Peter 5:8–9 calls believers to be sober and vigilant, resisting the devil steadfast in the faith.
And Ephesians 6:10–18 calls Christians to be strong in the Lord, put on the whole armor of God, stand against the devil's schemes, and persevere in prayer.
Notice the source of strength.
“Be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might.” — Ephesians 6:10, KJV
Not strong in your volume.
Not strong in your spiritual reputation.
Not strong in your ability to appear fearless.
Strong in the Lord.
The devil is not overcome by your performance of confidence.
The believer stands by depending on the God whose truth is trustworthy, whose righteousness matters, and whose salvation is found in Christ.
So yes, resist the devil.
Resist his lies with God's truth.
Resist temptation rather than entertaining it.
Resist the accusation that a repentant sinner can never be forgiven.
Resist the pride that whispers you do not need correction.
Resist the despair that says there is no reason to come home.
But do not forget the first command.
Submit yourselves to God.
Because you cannot faithfully resist the devil while deliberately embracing the rebellion he encourages.
And perhaps the most dangerous form of spiritual deception is not the person who openly admits they are far from God.
Perhaps it is the person who has learned enough Christian language to avoid asking whether their own heart is surrendered.
They know the songs.
They know the verses.
They know when to say amen.
They know how to recognize a powerful sermon.
But somewhere beneath the familiar words, a quiet question remains unanswered.
“Lord, is there something I am still refusing to give You?”
That question is not only for people who have fallen into public scandal.
It is for the respectable believer.
The longtime church member.
The Bible teacher.
The exhausted parent.
The young Christian fighting temptation.
The ministry leader who has begun confusing public usefulness with private faithfulness.
It is for me.
It is for you.
Because none of us outgrows our need for grace.
And none of us reaches a place where obedience becomes optional.
Maybe this article is reaching you in a season when you are tired of pretending.
You still believe in Jesus.
You still want to love Him.
But you have been fighting the same battle for so long that you hardly know how to talk about it anymore.
You have promised to change.
You have failed.
You have prayed.
You have cried.
You have wondered whether God is disappointed every time He hears your voice.
And perhaps the hardest thing is that you no longer trust your own promises.
Then stop making your promises the foundation of your hope.
Look to Jesus Christ.
His mercy is greater than your ability to explain yourself.
His power is not exhausted by your weakness.
His invitation to repent is not an invitation to earn your way back into His presence.
Come to Him truthfully.
Do not call sin harmless.
Do not call bondage freedom.
Do not call pride discernment.
Do not call revenge justice.
Do not call spiritual numbness peace.
But do not call yourself hopeless when Christ is still calling sinners to repentance.
The Gospel does not tell you that you are strong enough to save yourself.
It tells you that Jesus is a sufficient Savior.
And there is a difference between being convicted by the Holy Spirit and being crushed by hopeless condemnation.
Godly sorrow leads toward repentance, as 2 Corinthians 7:10 teaches.
The enemy's accusations seek to drive people into despair, concealment, and unbelief.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
That does not make sin trivial.
It makes the finished work of Christ precious.
The person who belongs to Jesus can confess sin without pretending that sin is their ultimate identity.
They can face the truth without believing the lie that redemption is impossible.
They can rise again, not because they are naturally invincible, but because the grace of God continues to work in them.
So tonight, or whenever these words find you, do something more important than simply agreeing with this article.
Find a quiet moment.
Put the distractions aside.
Open James chapter 4.
Read the whole passage.
Ask God to search your heart.
And when something comes to mind that you know you need to confess, do not immediately defend it.
Bring it before Him.
If you have wronged someone, consider what honest repentance and appropriate restitution require.
If you are trapped in a destructive pattern, seek trustworthy Christian accountability and the practical help you need.
If you have drifted away from Christ, return to the Gospel.
And if you have never placed your faith in Jesus, hear His call to repent and believe the good news.
You do not have to invent a more impressive version of yourself before coming to Him.
You need the Savior who died and rose again.
Perhaps your prayer could begin here:
“Father, I have spent so much time asking You to change my circumstances while resisting the ways You want to change my heart.
I have blamed others when I needed to repent.
I have defended things Your Word has called me to surrender.
I have sometimes wanted the comfort of Your promises without the correction of Your truth.
Forgive me.
Thank You for sending Jesus Christ to die for sinners and rise again.
I cannot cleanse myself. I cannot rescue myself. I cannot build a righteous life apart from Your grace.
Teach me to submit to You.
Give me strength to resist temptation, courage to confess what I have hidden, humility to make things right where I can, and faith to keep following Jesus when obedience is costly.
Let my life glorify You, not merely through the words I speak, but through the truth I believe and the way I live.
In Jesus' name, amen.”
And if that prayer expressed something you have been carrying silently, I want you to know that you are not the only person fighting a battle nobody sees.
There are people reading these words who are trying to rebuild a marriage.
People who are struggling with secret habits.
People who have wounded someone they love.
People who have been hurt by others and are learning that forgiveness does not require pretending the harm was acceptable or abandoning wise boundaries.
People who want to follow Jesus but feel overwhelmed by how much still needs to change.
There is room for honest conversation here.
You do not need to disclose private sins or painful details publicly. God knows what is behind those few words.
Not simply to increase the reach of a page.
But because someone among your friends may know how to quote “resist the devil” while quietly struggling to surrender something that is destroying their peace.
Someone may be drifting from Jesus.
Someone may be living behind a carefully maintained religious appearance.
Someone may be convinced that their failure has already disqualified them from mercy.
You may never know who reads what you share.
But a simple act of sharing can place Scripture before someone who needs to hear it.
Not because these words possess any special power, but because the Scripture they point to deserves more than a passing glance.
Return to James 4 when pride begins to rise, when temptation becomes persuasive, or when you find yourself more interested in fighting everyone else than surrendering your own heart to God.

We want this community to be a place where Scripture is taken seriously, Jesus Christ remains central, repentance is never separated from grace, and wounded people are pointed toward the hope of the Gospel.
And there is another invitation I want to make, with gratitude and without pressure.
But I want to be careful with something important.
The Bible teaches that giving should be willing and sincere.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Your local church, your family responsibilities, and the needs God has placed before you matter. Your giving should be prayerful and responsible.
What I can say is this:
When you voluntarily support faithful Gospel work, you help make that work possible.
You help create room for more biblical teaching, more Christian encouragement, more resources, and more opportunities to reach people who may otherwise never encounter these messages.
The Gospel itself is not for sale.
The grace of God is not behind a paywall.
We want people to have access to resources that encourage them to read Scripture, understand the Gospel, develop spiritual discipline, and keep growing in faith.
These products are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
They are simply another way to encourage faith, share biblical truth, and help sustain the work.
You can still help.
Pray for this ministry.
Help someone find the free resources.
Every genuine act of encouragement and every faithful conversation about Jesus matters, whether money is involved or not.
Because the goal is not to build a community of people who merely admire powerful Christian writing.
The goal is to point people toward Jesus Christ, who alone saves.
And now, before you leave, I want to bring you back to where we began.
There is a reason James begins with surrender.
Because the greatest need of the human heart is not to become impressive at spiritual warfare.
It is to be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ and to live under His gracious lordship.
The devil is real.
Temptation is real.
Spiritual opposition is real.
But so is human pride.
So is self-deception.
So is the stubbornness that makes us want God's protection while refusing His correction.
And so is the grace that meets repentant sinners at the foot of the cross.
Maybe you came into this article wanting to learn how to make the devil flee.
And perhaps God is using His Word to show you something more personal.
A conversation you need to have.
A sin you need to confess.
A grudge you need to release.
A habit you need to confront.
A lie you need to stop believing.
A Savior you need to trust.
Do not confuse reading about surrender with surrendering.
Do not confuse feeling convicted with repenting.
Do not confuse knowing the right verse with obeying the God who gave it.
You may be able to hide your struggle from the people who admire you.
But you do not have to hide from the One who already knows you completely.
The same Jesus who restored Peter is still mighty to save.
The same Gospel that brought hope to sinners in the first century still calls sinners to repentance and faith today.
The same Lord who commands you to stand against the devil also offers grace to the humble.
So surrender.
Not because God is cruel.
But because Jesus Christ is worthy.
Resist the devil.
Not because you are powerful on your own.
But because your strength is in the Lord.
Draw near to God.
Not because your past is spotless.
But because Christ has opened the way for sinners to receive mercy.
And when you fall, do not build a home in your shame.
Confess.
Repent.
Return to Christ.
Walk in His truth.
Keep following Him.
Because the story of your life does not have to end at the scene where you failed.
The place where your sin told you the story was over may become the very place where you finally understand how desperately you need the Savior.
